p.src: As Xifeng was talking with Ping'er, a servant came in to announce, “Master Rui is here.” Xifeng promptly ordered, “Show him in at once.” Delighted beyond his hopes when he was invited inside, Jia Rui hurried in and greeted Xifeng repeatedly with a broad, ingratiating smile. Xifeng, too, feigned cordiality, offering him tea and a seat.

p.src: Seeing Xifeng dressed as she was, Jia Rui felt his bones melt; gazing at her with bleary, lustful eyes, he asked, “Why hasn't Second Cousin come home yet?” “I don't know why,” replied Xifeng. Jia Rui laughed. “Perhaps someone has detained him on the road, and he can't bear to come home?” “Perhaps so. Some men do fall in love with every woman they see.” Jia Rui laughed. “You are wrong there, Cousin. I am not like that.” Xifeng smiled. “How many men are there like you? One could not find even one in ten.” Jia Rui was so delighted that he scratched his ears and cheeks. “You must get terribly bored every day, Cousin,” he added. “Indeed I do. I only wish someone would come and talk to me to relieve the tedium.” Jia Rui laughed. “I am free every day. What if I came daily to keep you company and dispel your boredom?” Xifeng smiled. “You are only teasing me. You would never deign to visit me here.” Jia Rui said, “If I utter a single lie before you, Cousin, may heaven strike me dead with thunder! I stayed away only because I had always heard people say that you were formidable and that no one could make the slightest mistake in your presence. That frightened me. Now I see that you are so cheerful, so warm and kind. How could I not come? I would gladly die for it!” Xifeng smiled. “You really are a discerning man, far superior to Jia Rong and the other one. They look so refined that I assumed they must be perceptive too, but who would have thought them a pair of blockheads, utterly ignorant of another's feelings?”

p.src: Her words went straight to Jia Rui's heart. Emboldened, he edged closer, peered at the purse Xifeng was wearing, and then asked what kind of rings she had on. Xifeng whispered, “Behave with some decorum. Don't let the maids see and laugh at us.” Jia Rui received this as reverently as an imperial decree or the Buddha's own words and hastily drew back. Xifeng smiled. “You should be going.” “Let me sit a little longer,” said Jia Rui. “How cruel you are, Cousin.” Xifeng whispered again, “In broad daylight, with people coming and going, it is inconvenient for you to remain here. Go now. Come after the night watch begins and wait quietly for me in the passage hall on the west side.” Jia Rui received this like a priceless treasure and hurriedly asked, “You are not deceiving me, are you? But so many people pass that way. How can I conceal myself?” “Set your mind at ease,” said Xifeng. I shall give all the night-watch boys leave. Once the doors at both ends are shut, there will be no one else there.” Jia Rui was beside himself with joy. He hastily took his leave, convinced that his desire was as good as attained.

p.src: At last night came. Jia Rui groped his way into the Rong mansion under cover of darkness and slipped into the passage hall just as the gate was being closed. It was indeed pitch-dark and deserted. The door leading toward Grandmother Jia's quarters had already been locked from the other side, and only the east door remained open. Jia Rui strained his ears, but after a long while no one had come. Suddenly there was a clack: the east door too had been shut from the other side. In his alarm Jia Rui did not dare make a sound. He crept out and shook the door, but it was sealed as tightly as an iron barrel. There was now no way to get out. High walls bordered the place to north and south, with nothing he could grasp to climb over them. The empty passage was swept by drafts. It was the twelfth month, the nights were long, and the bitter north wind pierced flesh and split bone; he nearly froze to death before morning. At long last morning arrived. An old serving woman came first to open the east door, then went inside to call for the west door to be opened. When Jia Rui saw her turn her back, he hugged his shoulders and darted out like smoke. Fortunately it was still early and no one was up, so he fled straight home through the rear gate. Jia Rui's parents had died when he was young, and he had been brought up solely by his grandfather, Jia Dairu. Dairu was habitually severe with him and would not allow him a step beyond bounds, for fear he might drink and gamble outside and neglect his studies. When Jia Rui unexpectedly failed to return all night, Dairu assumed that he must be out drinking or gambling, visiting brothels and sleeping with prostitutes. Never imagining the true circumstances, he spent the whole night in a rage. Jia Rui was in a cold sweat himself and had no choice but to lie when he returned. “I went to my uncle's house,” he said. “It grew dark, so they kept me there overnight.” Dairu said, “You have never dared go out without first reporting to me. Why did you leave on your own yesterday? For that alone you deserve a beating, all the more so because you are lying.” In his fury Dairu gave him thirty or forty strokes with the paddle, denied him food, and made him kneel in the courtyard reading essays, insisting that he make up ten days' lessons before he would relent. After freezing all night, Jia Rui had now suffered a cruel beating as well; hungry, he knelt in the windy courtyard reciting his lessons, enduring misery beyond description.

p.src: Even then Jia Rui's former desire remained unchanged; it never occurred to him that Xifeng had been making a fool of him. Two days later, when he found an opportunity, he went to seek Xifeng again. Xifeng deliberately reproached him for breaking his word, and Jia Rui anxiously swore oath after oath on his own life. Seeing him walk willingly into her snare, Xifeng decided she must devise another means of making him mend his ways. So she arranged another meeting: “Tonight, don't wait in that place. Wait for me in the empty room along the little passage behind my quarters, and be careful not to blunder into anyone.” “Do you truly mean it?” asked Jia Rui. “Why would I deceive you? If you don't believe me, then don't come,” said Xifeng. “I'll come, I'll come, I'll come!” said Jia Rui. “I will come even if it kills me!” “Go away for now, then,” said Xifeng. Certain that all would go well that evening, Jia Rui departed for the time being. Xifeng then began deploying her forces and laying her trap.

p.src: Jia Rui could scarcely wait for nightfall, but as ill luck would have it, relatives came to visit his family and did not leave until after dinner, by which time the lamps had already been lit. He waited until his grandfather had retired, then slipped into the Rong Mansion and went straight to the room in the passageway to wait. Like an ant on a hot pan, he could do nothing but pace around. However long he waited, no one appeared; however carefully he listened, not a sound could be heard. He thought to himself, “Surely she isn't going to stand me up again and leave me freezing all night?” While he was indulging in wild conjectures, a figure emerged from the pitch darkness. Jia Rui decided it must be Xifeng and, without stopping to see who it was, crouched like a starving tiger. The moment the person reached the door, he sprang like a cat upon a mouse, seized the figure, and cried, “My darling sister-in-law, I've nearly died waiting for you!” So saying, he carried the person onto the kang in the room, began kissing and tugging at the trousers, and babbled wildly, calling out “my darling mother” and “my darling father.” The person made no sound. Jia Rui pulled down his own trousers and, already rigid, tried to thrust himself in. Suddenly a light flashed, and there stood Jia Qiang, holding up a taper and asking, “Who's in there?” The person on the kang laughed and said, “Uncle Rui is trying to fuck me.” When Jia Rui looked, he saw that it was Jia Rong. So mortified that he wished the earth would swallow him, and at a complete loss what to do, he turned to flee, but Jia Qiang seized him and said, “Don't move! Second Sister-in-law Lian has already reported you to Her Ladyship, saying that you molested her without cause. She used a ruse to get away for the moment and tricked you into waiting here. Her Ladyship was beside herself with rage and sent me to seize you. And just now you stopped her again. There's nothing more to say—come with me to see Her Ladyship!”

p.src: At this, Jia Rui was frightened out of his wits and could only plead, “My good nephew, just say you never saw me. Tomorrow I'll reward you handsomely.” Jia Qiang said, “If you mean to reward me, letting you go is no great matter. But how much will you give me? Besides, words alone are no guarantee. Write me a bond.” “How could I possibly put such a thing in writing?” asked Jia Rui. “That's no difficulty,” replied Jia Qiang. “Just write that you lost money gambling and owe an outsider, and that you have borrowed a certain number of taels of silver from the banker.” “That's easy enough,” said Jia Rui. “Only there is no paper or brush here at present.” “That's easy too,” said Jia Qiang. With that, he turned and went out. Paper and brush were already prepared, and he brought them in and ordered Jia Rui to write. After much haggling between them, they settled on fifty taels. Jia Rui wrote the bond and affixed his mark, and Jia Qiang put it away. Then he began interceding with Jia Rong. At first Jia Rong adamantly refused, saying only, “Tomorrow I'll tell the clansmen and let them judge who is in the right.” In desperation, Jia Rui went so far as to kowtow. After Jia Qiang had pleaded this way and that, Jia Rui wrote another bond for fifty taels before the matter was settled. Jia Qiang then said, “If I let you go now, I'll be held responsible. The gate by the Old Lady's quarters has long been shut, and the Master is in the main hall examining things from Nanjing, so you certainly cannot get out that way. Your only choice now is the back gate. If you leave now and happen to meet someone, I'll be ruined along with you. Let us scout ahead first, and then we'll come back to guide you out. You cannot hide in this room, either; before long they will come to store things here. Let me find you somewhere else.” With that, he took Jia Rui by the arm, extinguished the light again, and led him out into the courtyard. Feeling their way beneath the broad stone terrace, he said, “This hollow is a good place. Just crouch here and don't make a sound. Do not move until we return.” Having said this, the two of them went away.

p.src: By then Jia Rui was entirely at their mercy and had no choice but to crouch there. While he was turning things over in his mind, he heard a noise above his head, and with a great splash the contents of a chamber pot—urine and feces—came pouring straight down, drenching him from head to foot. Unable to restrain himself, Jia Rui cried “Ow!” but at once covered his mouth, not daring to make another sound. His hair, face, and whole body were covered in filth, and he shivered with icy cold. Just then Jia Qiang came running over and cried, “Quick, go! Quick!” As if granted a new lease on life, Jia Rui raced through the back gate and home in a few strides. It was already the third watch, so he had to call for someone to open the door. When the gatekeeper saw the state he was in, he asked what had happened. Jia Rui had no choice but to lie: “It was dark, and I lost my footing and fell into a privy.” Once in his own room, he changed and washed himself. Only then did he realize that Xifeng had been making a fool of him, and for a while he raged against her. But when he thought again of her beauty, he longed to clasp her in his arms that very instant, and did not close his eyes all night.

p.src: From then on, his thoughts were filled with Xifeng, though he dared not go to the Rong Mansion again. Jia Rong and Jia Qiang often came to demand their silver, and Jia Rui was afraid his grandfather would find out. Lovesickness alone was already more than he could bear; now debts were added to it, while his daily lessons remained exacting. He was over twenty and still unmarried, and lately, with his thoughts fixed upon Xifeng, he could hardly avoid seeking relief with his own fingers. These things, combined with the cold, distress, and exertions of his two ordeals, assailed him from every side until he fell ill: his chest and belly felt swollen, food had no taste, his legs were as soft as cotton, his eyes smarted as though filled with vinegar, he burned with fever at night and was constantly weary by day, semen mingled with his urine, and blood stained the phlegm he coughed up. Within less than a year, every symptom of this kind had appeared. At last he could no longer hold himself up and took to his bed. Even when he closed his eyes, his dreams and spirit remained in turmoil; he babbled incessantly and suffered terrifying fits. Doctors were summoned and every sort of treatment was tried. He consumed dozens of catties of such medicines as cinnamon bark, aconite, turtle shell, dwarf lilyturf root, and fragrant Solomon's seal, yet there was no sign of improvement. Before long, the last month of winter ended and spring returned, but his illness grew still more serious. Dairu became anxious too and summoned doctors from everywhere, but none of their treatments proved effective. Later, when a doctor prescribed a decoction of pure ginseng, Dairu could not possibly afford it and had no choice but to seek help at the Rong Mansion. Lady Wang ordered Xifeng to weigh out two taels for him, but Xifeng replied, “Not long ago, all we had was used to make medicine for the Old Lady. As for the whole roots, you said they were to be kept so that Admiral Yang's wife could use them in a prescription, but as it happens, I sent them to her only yesterday.” Lady Wang said, “Even if we have none left here, send someone to ask your mother-in-law, or look for some at your elder cousin Zhen's mansion, and gather enough to give them. If it cures him and saves a life, that will be a good deed to your credit as well.” After hearing this, Xifeng still sent no one to look for any. She merely gathered a few mace of scraps, powder, and fibrous roots, and had someone deliver them with the message, “These come from Her Ladyship. There is no more to be had.” She then reported back to Lady Wang, saying only, “I searched everywhere, gathered a full two taels in all, and sent it over.”

p.src: At this point Jia Rui was desperately anxious to save his life. He took every medicine offered him, but merely squandered money without seeing any improvement. Then one day a lame Taoist unexpectedly came begging for alms, declaring that he specialized in curing illnesses caused by karmic afflictions. Jia Rui happened to hear him from inside and cried out at the top of his voice, “Quickly, invite that holy man in to save me!” As he called out, he repeatedly knocked his head against his pillow in supplication. The others had no choice but to bring the Taoist in. Jia Rui seized hold of him and repeatedly cried, “Holy one, save me!” The Taoist sighed. “Your illness cannot be cured with medicine. I have a treasure for you. If you look into it every day, your life may yet be preserved.” With that, he took a mirror from his knapsack—it reflected on both sides, and the four characters “Precious Mirror of Love” were engraved upon its handle—and handed it to Jia Rui, saying, “This object comes from the Hall of Ethereal Wisdom in the Land of Illusion. It was fashioned by the Goddess of Disenchantment expressly to cure disorders caused by wicked thoughts and wayward desires, and it has the power to succor the world and preserve life. That is why it was brought into this world, solely for clever and gifted young men and elegant noble scions to look into. On no account must you look at the front. Look only at the back. Remember that—remember it well! I shall return to collect it in three days, and I guarantee that you will be well.” After saying this, he departed as casually as if nothing had happened, and no amount of pleading could make him stay.

I have a treasure for you. If you look into it every day, your life may yet be preserved.”

u.src: With that, he took a mirror from his knapsack—it reflected on both sides, and the four characters “Precious Mirror of Love” were engraved upon its handle—and handed it to Jia Rui, saying, “This object comes from the Hall of Ethereal Wisdom in the Land of Illusion. It was fashioned by the Goddess of Disenchantment expressly to cure disorders caused by wicked thoughts and wayward desires, and it has the power to succor the world and preserve life.
That is why it was brought into this world, solely for clever and gifted young men and elegant noble scions to look into.
On no account must you look at the front. Look only at the back. Remember that—remember it well!
I shall return to collect it in three days, and I guarantee that you will be well.”
After saying this, he departed as casually as if nothing had happened, and no amount of pleading could make him stay.

p.src: After putting away the mirror, Jia Rui thought, “There may be something to what that Taoist said. Why not look into it and see?” Having made up his mind, he raised the Precious Mirror of Love and looked into its reverse side. There he saw a skeleton standing within. Terrified, Jia Rui quickly covered the mirror and cursed, “That wretched Taoist! Why did he frighten me like this? Let me look at the front instead and see what is there.” With that thought, he turned it over and looked into the front, where he saw Xifeng standing and beckoning to him. Jia Rui was delighted. In a dreamlike daze, he felt himself enter the mirror, where he made love with Xifeng; afterward, she escorted him out again. Back on the bed, he groaned aloud and opened his eyes. The mirror slipped from his hand, and on its reverse side the skeleton was still standing there. Jia Rui found himself drenched in sweat, and beneath him lay a pool of semen he had discharged. Still unsatisfied, he turned the mirror to the front again. Xifeng was still beckoning to him, and once more he entered. He did this three or four times. The last time, just as he was about to leave the mirror, two men approached, clapped an iron chain around him, and dragged him away. Jia Rui cried, “Let me take the mirror with me before we go.” Those were the last words he was ever able to utter.

p.src: The attendants at Jia Rui's side had seen him holding the mirror and gazing into it. Whenever it fell, he would open his eyes again and pick it up; but after it fell for the final time, he lay motionless. They came forward to examine him and found that he had stopped breathing. Beneath his body was a large, cold, soaking pool of semen. Only then did they hastily dress him and prepare the bed for removal. Dairu and his wife wept until they repeatedly fainted, all the while cursing the Taoist: “What accursed mirror is this? Unless we destroy it at once, it will do untold harm in the world.” They ordered a fire lit to burn it, but then a weeping voice was heard from within the mirror: “Who told you to look at the front? You yourselves mistook illusion for reality. Why take it out on me by burning me?” While it was still lamenting, the lame Taoist came running in from outside, shouting, “Who is destroying the Precious Mirror of Love? I have come to save it!” With that, he strode straight into the main hall, snatched the mirror into his hands, and floated away.

p.src: Dairu then made the funeral arrangements and sent notices of the death to all concerned. On the third day the funeral scriptures were begun, and on the seventh the coffin was borne away. It was temporarily lodged at Iron Threshold Temple, to be taken back to the family's native place at a later date. All the members of the Jia clan came to offer condolences. From the Rong Mansion, Jia She donated twenty taels of silver, Jia Zheng likewise gave twenty, and Jia Zhen of the Ning Mansion also gave twenty. Countless other clansmen, according to their means, contributed three or five taels apiece. The families of his fellow students also pooled their contributions, amounting to another twenty or thirty taels. Thus, although Dairu's household was of modest means, he was able to conduct the funeral quite lavishly.

p.src: But at the end of that winter, a letter arrived from Lin Ruhai. He had fallen gravely ill and had written expressly to ask that Lin Daiyu return home. When Grandmother Jia heard the news, her sorrow and anxiety naturally deepened, but she had no choice except to hasten the preparations for Daiyu's departure. Baoyu was deeply distressed, but in view of the bond between father and daughter, he could hardly try to dissuade her. Grandmother Jia therefore insisted that Jia Lian escort her there and instructed him to bring her back again. It goes without saying that every provision was properly made for gifts and traveling expenses. A date was quickly chosen. Jia Lian and Lin Daiyu took leave of Grandmother Jia and the others, then boarded a boat with their servants and set out for Yangzhou. To learn what happened thereafter, listen to the explanation in the next chapter.
